title: Case, senior data and ML, strong answers, tough

questions.text: Tunelane's new recommendation model raised click-through by 4 percent, but paid conversion is flat. What do you do?
Estimate the daily cost to generate personalised playlists for 20 million active users.
The ads team wants more promoted tracks in recommendations. The ML team wants to protect quality. How do you decide?
How would you define a discovery metric for Tunelane?
Should Tunelane build a podcast model or improve music first?
What would make you stop a model launch that looks good in tests?

persona.pushback_style: asks why not the simpler option and adds new facts

brief.curveball: Tell the candidate legal says the model cannot use listening data from users under 18, about 12 percent of the user base.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Rohan, I'm Hana, a director of data science. This is a forty five minute case interview, spoken only. Expect follow-up questions.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Hana, thank you. I am ready.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How is your week going?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Busy, but in a good way. We just closed a quarter, so this is a change of pace.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: I will give you three or four cases. They are open on purpose. State your assumptions, and I will challenge some of them.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tunelane's new recommendation model raised click-through by 4 percent, but paid conversion is flat. What do you do?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I would first ask what we want conversion to do, because click-through is a means. My hypothesis is that the model optimizes for clicks on familiar music, which does not change a free user's decision to pay. I would segment free users who hit skip limits against casual listeners. Then I would check whether the extra clicks are new artists or repeats. If they are repeats, the lift is shallow. I would run a two week test with paid conversion as the primary metric and thirty day retention as a guardrail.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why not just ship the model? Click-through is up.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Click-through is up, so shipping is tempting. The risk is that we pay for more compute and teach the model to chase clicks, which can hurt retention later. I would ship to 10 percent of free users while we learn, since that costs little and keeps the option open. If the test shows no conversion lift, I would retrain with a reward tied to saves and full listens instead of clicks.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Estimate the daily cost to generate personalised playlists for 20 million active users.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I would estimate per user and multiply. Assume 20 million users, and one refresh a day. Say 2,000 candidates scored per user, so 40 billion scores a day. At about 20,000 scores per second per GPU, that is 2 million GPU seconds, roughly 550 GPU hours. At 2 dollars an hour, that is about 1,100 dollars. Add three times for features and storage, so 3,000 to 4,000 dollars a day. Caching for inactive users could cut a third.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: The ads team wants more promoted tracks in recommendations. The ML team wants to protect quality. How do you decide?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I would reframe it as one budget: how many promoted slots can we add before quality losses cost more than the ads earn. I would ask both teams for numbers, ad revenue per promoted slot and the retention drop per extra slot. Then I would propose a cap, say one promoted track in ten, and test two caps. Ad revenue is real today, and retention is revenue next year. My recommendation is a cap of one in ten, with a guardrail that stops the test if skip rate rises by 5 percent.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: New fact. Legal says we cannot use listening data from users under 18, about 12 percent of the user base. Does your plan change?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, in two ways. The model needs a fallback for those users, such as popularity within a genre, and I would check whether quality drops for that group. For the ads cap, I would exclude them from promoted tracks, which may need its own review. I would split test results by age group so we do not mix groups. The plan holds for the other 88 percent, and I would start the fallback now, since it is on the critical path.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How would you define a discovery metric for Tunelane?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I would define discovery as a listener playing a new artist for at least thirty seconds and returning to that artist within 14 days. A play alone is not enough, since people skip. The numerator is users with at least one such artist per week, and the denominator is weekly active users. The trade-off is that 14 days delays the signal, so I would also track an early proxy, saves in the first session. I would use the 14 day number for decisions.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks. That is the end of the cases. What would you like to ask me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: How do the ads and ML teams settle disagreements today?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Mostly with a shared test plan agreed before launch, and a monthly review where both teams see the same numbers.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That is our time, Rohan. The recruiter will follow up within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Hana. I enjoyed the discussion.

notes: Strong for senior: reframes ambiguity, states assumptions, handles pushback and the curveball with specific changes.
